utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Toma Fila, I appear with Mr. Petrovic and Miss Lopicic for Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me well? Thank you. Before we start, let me tell you that the Registry has informed us that we can work in the week of 18 May on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday morning, so we would sit on Monday and Tuesday from 9.30 to 12.30 and from 2.30 to 5.30, whereas on Wednesday, we have only half a day from 9.30 to 12.30. I hope this is convenient for you. We now move on to our next witness. May I ask you to please stand up and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you asked two questions yesterday -- you personally -- concerning the composition of the Government and the appointment of the Ministries. The Defence has brought two laws to you -- they are not related to this particular witness. I would like to tender them in evidence if the Prosecution agrees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Both Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, both the Serbian and English versions. It refers to the questions asked yesterday by the judge. Could this be marked as the Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit D59 and the translation D59A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So two documents, two numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the other will be D60.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should first of all like to ask for the two documents that we tendered a moment ago whether the Prosecution has any objection. If not, may they be adopted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have not seen them, your Honour -- I am waiting for them -- no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be D59 and D60. Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed. WITNESS DC Examined by MR. PETROVIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to show the witness this piece of paper so that she can acknowledge whether it is her name on the piece of paper (Handed). I suppose the witness will be given the pseudonym of DC. I should like to ask the Witness DC to tell us whether, on 18 September 1997, she talked to interviewer Miroslav Vasic and did she, on that occasion, make and sign the statement that I am going to present her with now. Will you show the witness? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D62 and the English translation D62A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections, then I move that this be accepted and admitted as D62. I should like to ask Witness DC first of all to tell us whether she has completed the Higher School of Economics, where and when, and to introduce herself in short?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed the Higher School of Economics in Vukovar in 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What job did you perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Secretariat for Economic Affairs as a senior planner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Slavko Dokmanovic since 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about whether you know when Slavko Dokmanovic was elected President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was elected at the first multi-Party elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did he perform that function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He performed that function until May 1991. After that he was prevented from doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in greater detail how and who prevented him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he was elected in 1990, he performed his function until 1991, in May, and in 1991, in May, the disturbances began, and he was no longer able to go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a concrete case of preventing him to reach his work post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were several threats -- a lot of cases of this kind, and they were very frightening and so he was prevented from coming to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at that time in Vukovar -- at the time we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are speaking about the time after May, that is to say, mid May, up until I was in Vukovar, let us say that in the municipality they brought some people wearing masks -- they were not the police -- and these individuals searched everybody upon entrance, even the deputies themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these individuals, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I learned of this later on, because they had camouflage uniforms and I heard that they were members of the national guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A series of events took place afterwards -- shops were blown up, houses were shot at, fired at, people disappeared -- people were replaced at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any particular cases in which people were replaced at work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. For example, the director -- the then director of the radio station was replaced as well as the Secretary for National Defence, the director of Borovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why and who replaced them -- who removed them from office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic had performed the duties of President of the Assembly until that time. He was replaced by Mr. Vidic and the Assembly of the time, which met, made these changes -- their members, their deputies and up until then it was the Serbs that held these functions. Afterwards, their own people were appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know something about the replacement of the editor in chief of the Vukovar papers and Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also know that this happened in May, in view of the fact that it was my father in fact -- he was suspended and then he received, in July, a decree saying that he was relieved of his duties -- it was a retroactive decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we dwell or stop for a moment. I would like to show you some documents and we will go on to comment on them later on. Will you show the document to the witness, please. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D63 and the English translation D63A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. This other document as well, please. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D64, English translation D64A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what those documents contain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a telegram which states that the Ministry of Information allows the broadcasting of the present Radio Vukovar under the new name, the Croatian Radio Vukovar, and appoints a new director -- there is an error here -- he is not Mladen, he is Zdravko Seremet, who will take over his duties within 24 hours, immediately. Mr. Seremet has been appointed as the editor in chief -- the acting editor in chief following the suspension of Milan Covrko and Milan Stankovic and it is an official document and it is signed by the Minister, Hrvoje Hitrec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Ministry of Information of Croatia recalls the director of the Serbian radio who was a Serb national -- the second document, could you read out the date please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it was dated 4 May 1991. According to this document, once again from the Ministry of Information of the Republic of Croatia, there is information sent out which states the Ministry of Information of Croatia approves the broadcasting of Radio Vukovar under a new name, Croatian Radio Vukovar, and appoints Zdravko Seremet as its director. This decree comes into force immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there removals and replacement before Croatia proclaimed its independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with the former editor in chief of the Vukovar papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that decree relieving him of his duty followed, which on 30 July was handed to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at this document and tell us whether that is the document in question? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D65 and the English translation is D65A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not want to read out this decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, just comment on it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decree which arrived on 30 July 1991, by which my father, as the editor in chief of former Radio Vukovar, the Vukovar newspapers, was relieved of his duties, as of 6 May 1991. The decree is retroactive and, with that document, he was relieved of his duties. The explanation is given that Zdravko Seremet was appointed to replace him. I do not think there is any special comment that I can make there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of illustration of the atmosphere prevailing in Vukovar at the time, would you look at an article -- a newspaper article, which also relates to your father, and tell us what the article is about? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D66 and English translation D66A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an article from the "Slobodni Tjednik", published in Osijek on 28 June 1991. On the first page, it has the title, "Mirko Stankovic sentenced to death". I shall read out just one segment: "The one-time head of the Vukovar radio, now correspondent at Television Belgrade, has been sentenced to death on the part of the armed Croatian guerrilla. Five individuals have been assigned to carry out this sentence. He is a disinformer and instigates hatred. There are stories that he did not want to tell us anything precisely. There are two groups of five people that have been designated to liquidate Stankovic -- his house would have been blown up long ago but the house he is living in does not belong to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should like to tender D66 as evidence -- documents 63 to 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We would object to this. It is a newspaper article reporting on something. We do not know who this was written by or anything about the truthfulness of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have decided to admit it into evidence, although of course it is a press article with obvious limitations inherent in this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Vukovar on 22 July 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the circumstances under which you left Vukovar and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was threatened by phone in my home, and at my parents' house, the house was shot at three times and this caused fear and unrest and, therefore, we were forced to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to go back to 20 November 1991. Were you in Vukovar on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that you were in Vukovar on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19 November I was at VELEPROMET because my mother and grandmother were in the cellar throughout the duration of the war. I found my mother on the 19th and took her out, but as my husband and I were looking for my husband's aunt and uncle, we did not find them on the 19th and we took my parents to Sid and, on the 20th, once again, returned to VELEPROMET to look for my husband's aunt, because that is all the family that he has left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 20th, who did you see in the courtyard of VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw many people -- the people from the same town, people I knew. There were many people there at the VELEPROMET compound, because they had left the cellars after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see Slavko Dokmanovic and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Slavko in the courtyard of VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere around 2 o'clock -- 2 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we show the witness tape D2 -- would the witness tell us whether she recognises the events at VELEPROMET which can be seen on the tape? Is that the atmosphere that prevailed and are those the people who were present on the occasion? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you recognise somebody, please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already recognised someone. (Videotape continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us who you recognise, quite freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic, Slavko from the back side, Mr. Jaksic, my husband, Mr. Jaksic, that is my husband on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is sufficient, thank you. Was that the particular day and the people you saw on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on both counts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until up around half past 3 -- 3.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the courtyard the whole time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not in the courtyard the whole time. I said hello to the people I knew -- the ones that I mentioned -- and then I left them in the courtyard and I went into a room to get warm, because it was cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave VELEPROMET and what direction did you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I left at around half past 3 in the afternoon towards Negoslavci and Sid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop on the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stopped for a brief moment in the village of Negoslavci and, after that, somewhere in front of the village of Orolik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why in front of Orolik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a column of buses which moved in front of us and it had stopped, because they had been brought tea, some hot beverages and some food, and the column was there for a little over half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were all the people from VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we stayed there for some time, and my husband went out of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this -- what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, dusk was falling -- about 5 o'clock perhaps. My husband left the car to see whether we would be moving on soon, because nobody liked driving in the dark in those days, so he went out and he came back fairly quickly. He told me that there seemed to have been an incident of some kind, that Slavko had an incident with a policeman, an encounter with a policeman and that the whole thing ended peacefully and that they would be letting us through, so that we passed by the column of buses and moved in the direction of Sid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how Slavko Dokmanovic was dressed on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. I did not pay attention to what he was wearing, because I just said a brief hello to him and we continued -- I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the situation in that town today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you ask me honestly and if you want an honest answer, I think that it is even worse than it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I object. We are seven years past the event and the status of what is going on in Vukovar today is irrelevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The book that we have been discussing for several days was also published a long time after the events and we are spending at least one hour talking about it every day so we just want to illustrate the situation and the continuity of the relationship towards the Serb population in the town. I want to show two documents for illustration purposes, as to the relationship towards the Serbs before, during and after the events, but if the court considers this to be irrelevant, we will withhold that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, it is irrelevant. You were mentioning that book -- of course we have only seen some parts of the book -- those parts which have been translated into English, they are relevant because they relate to events back in 1991 and 1992, so therefore the reference to that book is not immaterial to our matter. I do not think that there is any relevance to the present issue we are discussing, so therefore can you explain to us what sort of documents these are before we decide whether or not to admit them into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The documents -- the first document is the sentence of an organisation of an Ustasha character, sentence passed over individuals, including Jacques Klein, who was the UNTAES administrator in the Srem Baranja region. The second is a document which was handed into the houses and letter boxes of the Serb nationals, with serious threats which later on made them leave Vukovar. Just for purposes of information -- just as an illustration -- perhaps you could have a look at them and then you will be able to decide whether you admit them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Time and again we have insisted that we are really only concerned with the facts and the legal issues surrounding the present indictment. So we do not want to take into account historical events which happened before or things which happened after the event with which we are concerned. Let me consult my colleagues. We cannot admit them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour, thank you. Cross-examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DC, you indicated, or the documents that have been introduced by the Defence indicate, that your father was suspended from his position on 4 May 1991; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was the telegram -- that was before the suspension which came in July, as I said, but it was backdated to May -- I think it was 5 May, or 6 May -- I am not sure now, because I do not have the paper here with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in any event, the decision was made on 5 or 6 May and that is when he was informed about it, although it did not officially occur until June or July; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was informed on 30 July and a telegram itself was not given to him at all, because he had been suspended before that time, so he was unable to go to work, so it was only on 30 July that he learned that he had been -- that his employment had been terminated and that it was backdated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was on 4 May then that he was suspended, is that correct, and it was only later that he was actually informed of the circumstances under which this had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, this was two days after the incident in Borovo Selo; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing during the course of the battle -- were you working during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- what battle are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vukovar -- in the autumn of 1991, the events that we are talking about here, were you working during the course of those two or three months when the fighting was going on in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody worked in Vukovar during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any type of employment outside of Vukovar during that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see Slavko Dokmanovic during that time period prior to 19 or 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 20 November, when you were at VELEPROMET, were you wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever wear a uniform at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have indicated that you were there looking for your husband's aunt; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you arrive at VELEPROMET, you and your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, around 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do in the period between 10 and 2 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already said, the courtyard of the VELEPROMET was full of people we knew -- Vukovar is a small town, we all know each other so I spent the entire time with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were just talking about things that had happened and what was going on on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out any information about your husband's aunt while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We received information that one part of the town from the River Vuka towards Borovo left to Dalj and the rest gathered in VELEPROMET and that is the reason why around 3.30 p.m. we went back to Sid in order to look for her on that side, so we had to go around to reach Dalj and to find her there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it was around 3.30 in the afternoon that you got this information that the people from north of the Vuka had been taken to Dalj; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that time -- obviously all your efforts to find her had been unsuccessful; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you and your husband anxious about locating her and what had happened to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since these are the only relatives left to my husband, because he does not have his parents any more -- they are not alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were unable to find your husband's aunt at the JNA barracks -- sorry, at VELEPROMET, did you go to the JNA barracks to look for her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, since we had learned that she had been unable to leave towards that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about prior to that time -- prior to 3.30, you were there for approximately five and a half hours and had been looking for her; during all of that period, when you were not able to locate her, you never made an effort to go and try and find her at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I did not know that there were any civilians in the barracks -- it never occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the JNA barracks at all on 20 November for any reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it would be untrue that you and your husband approached some buses -- they were lined up at the JNA barracks and your husband said in your presence to Emil Cakalic that he was on the wrong bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would also be your testimony that in reply to a question from Mr. Cakalic as to what was the right bus, your husband said, "It does not matter, they are all the same"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether my husband said that and my acquaintance with Mr. Cakalic is so frail, and we never went to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband knew Mr. Cakalic from having worked with them at the municipality though, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to give you a small piece of paper and ask you to write your maiden name on this piece of paper, if you would, please. I would enter this as the next Prosecutor's exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 203.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If it can be shown to the Defence as well. So, as I understand it, Witness DC, it is your testimony that you and your husband remained at VELEPROMET the entire time between 10 in the morning and approximately 3.30 in the afternoon -- correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you were in the courtyard for a while and then you went into this office. While you were in the office, do you know what was going on outside in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not really say -- I had gone into the building because I was cold, I had a hot tea and then my husband called me when we were about to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you saw Slavko Dokmanovic arrive around 2 p.m. Was he alone or was he accompanied by other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was accompanied by the persons I saw on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people that you saw on the film were ones that came in with him at 2 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say the names of the people that you saw him come in with -- you have pointed them out on the screen, but can you be more specific as exactly who you saw him with, those whose names you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic, Rade Leskovac, Goran Hadzic, Duskojakic, Mr. Cvetkovic -- I met him that day, as well as Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mr. Dokmanovic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a couple of words -- how his family was, how was he and that is what he asked me and that was all and then I left that area, because there was a large number of men and they were all talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just said hello.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way -- how do you know him, how long have you known him and in what context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him in the private capacity. We would not be able to discuss anything, but to exchange greetings -- that would be the extent of our acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he was wearing a military uniform on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice that anyone was wearing a uniform, because there was such a crush of people and the commotion -- we were all so upset and excited, because it was two days after the liberation, so many people had passed there and I cannot really recall who was wearing what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I put it to you that on the video we just viewed he was in some type of military uniform, would you be able to say why this was? If you wish, we can view the video, but I am just asking do you know one way or the other why he might have been in an uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to why, I could not say -- I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of a meeting which took place at VELEPROMET on 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have indicated that you saw Mr. Dokmanovic and that you spoke with him prior to going into the office. Did you see him again after you came out of the office, shortly before you left the VELEPROMET facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left VELEPROMET, where did you go exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We set off towards Negoslavci, we were behind the column of buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many cars were there in your group, or how many vehicles of the people leaving from VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact number, but the column was quite long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you located in this column -- near the front, near the middle, near the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, near the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was in your vehicle with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was just the two of you in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether we had given anyone a lift -- I really cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, as I understand it, you departed VELEPROMET and went straight from there to Negoslavci; where you stopped briefly; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then from Negoslavci to Orolik; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of Orolik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you arrive in Orolik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it may have been around quarter past 4 -- 4.15. We stopped there and we stayed there for maybe about half an hour, maybe even more -- since, as I said, the people on the buses were given hot beverages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Orolik, you said that your husband told you that there had been some type of incident in which Mr. Dokmanovic was involved; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see Mr. Dokmanovic or witness this incident that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was already dusk -- I did not leave the car. He had left the car to see how long we would be staying there, and, when he reached the barricade, he saw silhouettes of some people -- among others there was Mr. Dokmanovic, but at that time the incident had already been solved and military police officers let us through -- the whole column of cars -- we were allowed to pass by the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour. Re-examined by MR. PETROVIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one situation; did you see Slavko Dokmanovic get to the VELEPROMET compound or standing in the VELEPROMET compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him stand there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, I do not think this is really a question for the witness, but while it is in my mind, could you clarify it or help clarify this? It is in relation to the position of VELEPROMET in relation to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: VELEPROMET is located across the street from the JNA barracks and approximately -- somewhere between 100 and 400 metres south of the barracks in the direction of Negoslavci, so it is directly across -- sorry, it is across the street and then down somewhere between 100 and 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection to the Witness DC being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Witness DC, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Fila or Mr. Petrovic, are you suggesting that we are going to see the videotape?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You said yesterday that it is about two hours to view the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. It is two hours long, but only two or three minutes right at the beginning are very important, because there we can see who is what, but I repeat once again why it is important -- it is dated 1991, and Mr. Dokmanovic presents his views there. He did not know at that time that he would be facing trial now here before you in 1998, so the things that he is saying at that time are important for this court to see whether he is an extremist or not, or whether he was a member of the Serbian National Council or not, because it is evident from the tape -- we are talking about 1991 -- and the Prosecution witness Vidic Bili mentioned this tape and that is why I took that tape, to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We have no objection to the tape, but the copy that we received yesterday was only a 50-minute programme, so I am not sure if we have actually viewed the tape that he plans on showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies, Mr. Williamson. I do not want to appear to be lying, but I am just repeating what my investigators told me -- if you saw only 50 minutes, then it is just 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection then, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will now take a 10-minute recess and then we will come back and view the videotape. (10.50 a.m.) (A short break) (11.03 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can go ahead with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the man by the name of Ilija Petrovic, he is the author of the book proffered by Mr. Williamson. I do not mean Mr. Williamson's book, but the book shown by Mr. Williamson. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please note for the record that the interpreters do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Speaker: We have invited Ilija Petrovic, member of the National Council; Ilija Kuncarevic, Secretary-General of the Serbian National Council; Pero Matic, a teacher from Beli Manastir; Slavko Dokmanovic, the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar; Goran Hadzic, the President of the municipal committee of the Serbian Democratic Party for Vukovar, and a member of the main committee of the Serbian Democratic Party for Knin, and Caslav Ocic from Dalj. The Serbian National Council for Slovonia, Baranja and Western Srem was established this year in -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We did not see the beginning, I apologise. Can we please rewind to the beginning, so that we hear how the persons are introduced, because this has not been on the tape? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Speaker: We have invited to the studio Ilija Petrovic, member of the National Council; Ilija Kuncarevic, Secretary-General of the Serbian National Council; Pero Matic, teacher from Beli Manastir; Slavko Dokmanovic, the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar; Goran Hadzic, the President of the municipal committee of the Serbian Democratic Party for Vukovar, and a member of the main committee of the Serbian Democratic Party for Knin, and Caslav Ocic from Dalj. The Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem was established this year in Sidski Banovci at Christmas. Of course, the Orthodox Christmas. So far, of the members of the Serbian National Council we only knew the name of Ilija Koncarevic, the Secretary-General, and today we identify another member, Ilija Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic, why the secrecy surrounding the names of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason is quite simple. In Croatia we have an Ustasha regime, and we have seen what the scenario is according to which they work. It is logical that if they knew the names, they would also be on the list of people to be eliminated and that is why we thought it quite normal that the names of the remaining 19 members of the National Council be kept secret for the time being. The fact that the names have not been disclosed does not mean that the National Council is not operating. This Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem is fully operational and in the meantime they issued two proclamations and I hope that they will continue to do so. I have to add here that the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, as its name says, operates in a narrower area of what is today the Republic of Croatia and that it works in accordance with the declaration on the establishment of the Serbian National Council passed at the Convention, passed in Srb in July and now, because some of us have maybe forgotten something from geography we learned so far in the past, and maybe we were not at school that day, Western Srem, according to our views, extends from its eastern line, Ilok, Lovas, Sid, Tovarnik and Jamena, and to the west it is bordered by the line extending from Cepin down 15 kilometres to Slavonski Brod. Slavonia extends from that line, Cepin, Slavonski Brod, and to the west it is from the estuary of the river Ilova down to the Virovitica. Baranja can be most easily defined. It is the triangle edged by Drava and the Danube and by the Hungarian border, the border between Hungary and Yugoslavia. Question: Mr. Koncarevic, were you the most brave person, since you gave your name to the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. KONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not the most courageous one, it was simply necessary to do so. I spent most of my time in Slavonia and Baranja and also Krajina. The Council requested me to do so and I performed that task. In the proclamation on the establishment of the Serbian National Council it is stated as follows: faced with the fact that Slovenes and Croats have issued separate decisions on seceding from the State of Yugoslavia, which they joined, together with Serbs, in a joint decision, and the rights of the third partner, the Serbs, have been completely ignored, so that is the reason why Serbian National Council was formed. Question: Can you tell us something about the reasons why it was established in Sidski Banovci and why on Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KONCAREVIC
utterances.text: You have three questions, I will try to answer them in turn. We are a part of the Serbian National Council which was formed in Srb and this area that we cover is a geographically specific area -- the second question, why in Sidski Banovci -- there is a reason why. We wanted to show how absurd it is to draw some kind of (INAUDIBLE) borders which are now used by the HDZ as their own borders. So, Sid remains -- the western part of the municipality of Sid remains outside that area and it does not contain -- this area does not contain any of the surrounding villages, although it is logical that the Sidski Banovci village should be in Sid municipality and not in Vinkovci municipality as it is now, and that was the reason why we wanted to show just how absurd this is, by our choice of the location. Why on Christmas? Well, first of all we Serbs live according to the principles of Saint Sava. We are unable to wish ill on anyone and we cannot do anything bad to any other people, least of all on Christmas. In one of the paragraphs of our proclamation we called on our Croatian brothers to stop their Croatian "national fighters", in inverted commas, and to make them recognise their rights and to tell them that all the wars so far have ended in history and that the irrational of the Croatian national fighters against Serbia should stop. We also told him that the Serbian nation has its roots in this area and that the Serbian spirit remains there and we wanted to tell them that they should not do any harm to the Serbian people -- not do anything to the Serbian people that they would not wish the Serbian people to do to them. Question: Mr. Matic, Croatia reacted to the Serbian National Council by stating that Serbs wanted to make this area more Serbian -- is that true Mr. Matic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MATIC
utterances.text: Well, that is what they state, that is their view, but if you look at the history and if you know some facts, they have no reason to claim this, because Serbs have been present here since time immemorial -- many historical documents dating as far back as the 10th century testify as to the presence of Serbs in this area. However, since we are here linked mostly to Baranja and to Western Srem, I would like to stress once again the problems linked historically with this region. These are mostly Serbian areas. You will find in history, for instance, from Duke Rakoci in the 18th century, he calls the area from Balota to the place where the Drava River joined the Danube, "the Serbian land". Serbs never conquered this region, they inhabited, settled this area when they fled from the Turks and searched for new areas where they could recognise and realise their political existence. They found this area in Baranja and that is how they came to live here. The Serbian nation has full historical legitimacy, but, in a series of tragedies that befell the Serbian nation and many misfortunes, one of the misfortunes happened to them in 1946. It is well-known that, due to arbitrary political decisions, and this is what people who lived to see this region -- that Baranja and Western Srem came to be a part of Croatia, although we know that historically, before the First World War, this area belonged to the Danube Vojvodina, Danube Banovina and before that to southern Hungary and to Serbian Vojvodina. That is why this interpretation that we are making this country a Serbian place is not true, but Serbs have lived there for a long time -- they have their deeds to land to prove that, and unfortunately, in the past, in the last war, this has been stolen -- this property has been stolen from them. Question: Mr. Matic, you are from Beli Manastir and not Bijeli Manastir, so let us put right an error that occurred on the screen in the caption?

utterances.speaker: MR. MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, officially the name is Beli Manastir. Question: Mr. Dokmanovic, you are President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. Could you tell us what it means to be the President of the municipality of a town in HDZ rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Vukovar is an area where 23 nations and nationalities live. Until one year ago they lived fairly peacefully and that is how they should live. Vukovar is Yugoslavia in small and that is how everybody behaved. Nobody ever stressed their national and religious affiliation. This was never a hindrance of life together. Before the first multi-Party elections took place, the HDZ endeavoured, by all means available, to homogenise the Croat people and the people lived up to that and we had a division and this national tension is fairly evident, there is a lot of mistrust and the politics of the day -- the militant policy contributes to this, of the insurgent side and they are playing at the razor's edge and this can lead to serious incidents with unforeseeable consequences. In Vukovar at the elections these socialists were victorious, they have a significant majority in the Assembly. The work of the Assembly is evolving under fairly difficult conditions and I can tell you that it is a thankless task to be the President of the Municipal Assembly at this particular point where the leftist side has won. Question: Can you tell us as a Serb in the municipality whether you have -- there has been any coercion and pressure exerted on you and there were attempts to dismantle this. What is the situation like today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The overall economic situation has contributed to an even more difficult situation, together with the national situation, so the settling of accounts, which is taking place between the Serb leaders, it is a settling of accounts with the ancient regime, generally the Communists, and that is where the Serbs are mostly the victims. Question: Mr. Hadzic, you are President of the municipal council of Serbian Democratic Party, municipal committee of the SDS and it has been set up and you have been able to organise yourselves. From that aspect, tell us the position of the Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HADZIC
utterances.text: As you said yourself, we organised ourselves relatively late, but our Croatian -- by virtue of the acts of our Croatian brethren we had to organise ourselves. The position of the Serbian people is a very difficult one. I cannot say that the people are frightened -- after all, the events that have occurred -- we know that there was 1941 and 1945 and we have nothing to fear any more. After the constitution of Croatia, we have been wiped out as a people in these areas -- nothing remains apart from our head on our shoulders and life itself so we have nothing to fear any more, but perhaps we as individuals -- and we had a meeting last night and one of the conclusions was that while we are frightened that a part of the leadership and the presidency of the republic could make moves which are errors, we are afraid of something else, that is, the Croatian silence, and I think that, after that, nobody has distanced themselves from the events that have taken place. That is more frightening, because -- anybody can make a mistake, leaders can make a mistake but a nation must not make a mistake and I do not think this can be done by the Croatian people and they are our friends, they are our neighbours and we know that they arm themselves. We thought this was individual, but we are very sorry to see that nobody distanced themselves from these facts. Question: How does the Serbian nation explain recognition of the images that appeared? How do you explain the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it is tragic. It would be funny were it not tragic and that is why we find it difficult, because people are trying to justify themselves and that is absurd. Question: Mr. Ocic, the programme of Television Novi Sad is viewed in Slavonia and Baranja, and viewers very often call us and not only Serbs; the Croats too call us and tell us about the situation in Slavonia and Baranja and say the Serbs are rich there. You said something about the economic situation there. Let me remind you that the Serbs in Slavonia, Baranja, Croatia and Dalmatia were never serfs and they were a free enterprising people and they were always ready to undertake risks and that they were great entrepreneurs in the initial days of capitalism. In the 19th century, as I say, they were very good entrepreneurs, enterprising people both individually and collectively, and it is thanks to their entrepreneurial spirit they became rich. One of the largest banks in Croatia was the Serbian bank at the time. The Serbian "Compos" newspaper shows there were Serbian monetary funds and institutions on the territory of what was the Austro-Hungarian empire. Not only individually were they rich but they showed affiliation towards collective organisation. For example, there were many businessmen and entrepreneurs were trained systematically and there was a very important man at the time, Vladimir Matejevic, who was one of the individuals who systematically organised foundations and legacies and training for entrepreneurs. One of the reasons for this irrational hatred of the Serbs was this spirit of entrepreneurship and their riches and their shops were destroyed in Zagreb. This can be compared to the pogroms against the Jews, so Serbs were very successful businessmen and talented and therefore fairly well-off. The attacks on Serbian property in the first war and Second World War was evident and destroyed much of the properties they had. The situation after the war was such that, through a regional policy, systematic -- organised colonisation was resorted to and people left for economic reasons -- came to urban environments and economic prerequisites for assimilation were set up in which they lost their national identity, and there was less possibility for Serbs, as opposed to the Austro-Hungarian empire where there was the fair play and the rule of law. They lost their economic status, the status that they had previously, so by isolating them communicationwise from other areas where Serbs lived and worked, gave rise to the economic prerequisites for separating them economically and nationally. The classical thesis that was supported before the war and is still supported is that we cannot with the form of autonomy for Serbs become organised because that is the HSS thesis -- as everything is repeated today, and history repeats itself so it is an association of the poor people. But if we look at natural resources and the human potential and everything else, then we can conclude that there is a very healthy, good foundation, economic foundation for all kinds of independent decision-making and taking one's fate in one's own hands. However, the situation of late is to undermine the economic background of the collective of Serbs in Croatia -- Serbs are being laid off and only those who are of a proper ethnic background are being employed -- Serbian personnel in charge of certain companies are being attacked, so this overall discrimination and the bringing into jeopardy of basic human rights is being conducted. These are not just situations on the verge of the incident -- this is State terrorism and Serbs are being deprived of their economic basis for their existence. Attempts to make something about that -- some kind of unofficial organisation, association of people -- for instance, in Dalj people tried to organise themselves in economic terms, encountered such fierce resistance and in all the media there were such fierce attacks against those people who just tried to fight for their own economic existence. The situation is so horrible -- the accusations are so horrible, so instead of enabling everybody, regardless of their religious or ethnic backgrounds, to live in economic terms, they attack the very existence, at the roots of the very existence. In Europe, virtually in the 21st century, we have this Nazification, the revival of fascism, because Croatia never went through the process of de-Nazification such as happened in Germany and it never accepted its status as a defeated power. It is incredible that we are seeing now this darkness again -- it is a systematic effort, striking at the very roots of the Serbian national identity. We promised that our viewers will also take part in our programme, we have somebody on the line."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, this is really inaudible. "Speaker: You are on the air. Caller: I wanted to ask a question of the gentleman from Knin. Since in this situation today we are discussing the future of Yugoslavia, I want to know why, today, representatives of the Knin Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina in the beginning said that they would have a united front regardless of the fact of whether Yugoslavia would be a federation or a confederation.
