Speaker: Obviously this is a question for Goran Hadzic, who is the President of the municipal committee of the Serbian Democratic Party for Vukovar and he is also a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, the main committee from Knin. Can you give us an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HADZIC
utterances.text: I will try to answer. I would like to thank the friendly advice. I do not know whether the viewer is aware of the fact that the province of Krajina has been proclaimed and we recognised it -- multi-Party elections in Bosnia were conducted and most of the Serbian people voted for SDS, which means that the Serbs are political people in Bosnia -- and recognised as such, as opposed to Croatia, and that was the reason why Krajina was formed. Our positions are clear. Serbian people will live in one State and that is Yugoslavia. For as long as this Yugoslavia exists, it is not necessary. In fact, Krajina was formed because Croatia erased the Serbian people from the constitution. Speaker: Mr. Koncarevic, you wanted to say something about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KONCAREVIC
utterances.text: You have to know that the Serbian people in Krajina, in Bosnia, is now in the Parliament, in the Government, it is a constituent people there, political people, and there is no reason to change anything there. As for this part of the nation which is in Croatia, they will have to articulate themselves through their political claims, through the Serbian National Council. A democratic politician said at one stage that everybody is for Yugoslavia if there is no other solution. It is possible that we may face this problem, too, and that one day we will face the question, what if Yugoslavia cannot survive? The Serbian people will probably have to take a very firm stand and to start the unification into a single Serbian State and for about six months I have been calling this State the Serbian land in the singular -- not the Serbian lands, because if we were to use the term "Serbian lands", that would make it possible for any of those areas or territories who were to join this State, to secede at one point once the passions have calmed down -- they would be able to say, "I am just one of the territories belonging to those lands", so from the very beginning we should clearly define the Serbian -- the borders of the Serbian State. At that point we will probably have to face the problem of how to achieve that. Everybody thinks there has to be a war. It does not have to be a war. We have had a war and Serbian people have paid the price. The people in power in Croatia today refer to the thousand years dreams and aspirations, they claim they are inheritors of the independent State of Croatia and we have to let them know quite clearly that the independent State of Croatia is the defeated side. They have lost the war, they have to sign the capitulation, they have to sign the armistice and the conditions of the armistice are dictated by the winning power and in this case the winning power, the victors are the Serbian people and the Serbian State. Speaker: Mr. Matic, whenever we start talking about Serbs living in a single State, the reactions in Croatia amount to -- they always say that Shiptars should also live in Albania. It is clear they do not admit there is a difference between ethnic minorities and nations. It is obvious that according to that theory Serbs are a national minority in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MATIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the latest constitution they adopted, Serbs are treated by them as a national minority. However, Serbs are a political people -- a political nation in that area. They have their territories -- of course, in the context of the State of the Yugoslav peoples you cannot talk about the Shiptar people. They cannot have the same rights as the Yugoslav peoples and we all know that Serbs are a Yugoslav people regardless of the areas where they lived in this country of ours, because we treat it as our country. But opinions differ and of course if any borders are to be drawn, especially between Serbs and Croats, because these are the areas that are most in dispute, if there should be a confederation or a break-up of Yugoslavia -- and Croatia has been really working on this -- we should not despair, because historical documents, if we use historical documents, the principle of history is on our side, international law is on the side of the State-forming people and that is the Serbian people in this case, and of course any ethnic interpretations that they can come up with when they put together apples and oranges in their media, that will not be of assistance to them, because the data from the census clearly speak -- of course, the census that we can rely on -- also indicate the ethnic principle will be on the side of the Serbian people. Speaker: Quite obviously there is a lot of interest from our viewers for this programme. We have someone on the line, good evening? Caller: I should like to congratulate the National Council for having given us their names, disclosed their names for the first time and I should like to ask a question related to borders, but before I go on to ask my question concerning the borders, I should like to ask comrade Dokmanovic to answer who organised the care of the Baranja children when they were sent to the Sombor municipality, that is to say, to the village of Prigravica, because there was a voice on Belgrade 202 television programme, radio programme. I should also like to talk about the borders of good old Serbia and I hope she will live on. I am -- there is a ransom on my head as well, I feel. We know the old borders of Serbia, Sombor towards Karlovac and Virovitica, and that is the most difficult situation today. Baranja never belonged to Croatia and I do not know what right in 1946 gave people the right to appropriate it. I consider Josip Broz to blame for this, but I also feel that the Serbian traitors or those who helped them were to blame. I now have a concrete question anybody can answer, and that is whether the borders of old Serbia -- are they possible in the present day and I should like to ask all of you individually a collective question: when we come to vote for Yugoslavia, or for another option, will you come out in favour of a united Serbia, or for Yugoslavia. I am in favour of a united Serbia and long live Serbia. May I have your answers please. Speaker: Mr. Matic, I feel that this is taking part in our discussion here, but can you answer the question -- can you answer our viewer? The gentleman, who did not give us his name for understandable reasons, brought up the question of the Baranja children and I will try to answer him as far as I am able, because I am not connected to any Party, I am outside parties fighting for the Serbian people, to the best of my ability, but this drive was organised by all the parties from Baranja in which the Serbian people are included, and for well-known reasons, if an explosive situation takes place which can lead to a civil war and which could have done so, at that particular time, to see that the children were safe, so this was an agreement and cooperation that existed between people in Backa and people in Baranja. As far as the second question is concerned about the borders, these are all ideas that we have in mind, and perhaps it is one of our tragedies that we did not think earlier in the way that we are thinking now, that our level of national awareness is now at its peak and it is possible and not possible to think about borders at the same time -- of the Serbia that we have -- greater or not. It is a fact that Baranja never belonged to Croatia, and neither did it belong to the independent Croatia that the leaders refer to. It was Hungary and finally Baranja was a component part of the Serb State. I have here the coat of arms -- for those who do not know this, that the Serb Vojvodina existed and what it united. Baranja, like Western Srem has its historical identity within the province of Vojvodina. On the right-hand side, you can -- the photograph is very bad but you can see the pictorial representation of Srem -- it is the deer symbolising Srem, on the opposite side is the lion symbolising Banat and on the right-hand side is a maiden representing Backa and the lamb on the other side symbolising Baranja. There we have the coat of arms of Serbian Vojvodina and it is very relative to ask how long it lasted, but it did exist, and it has its historical identity. Speaker: Mr. Dokmanovic, part of the question was addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This question -- the answer was supplied to the question by Mr. Matic about the children from Beli Manastir. I am President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. I do not know the situation there and if the information satisfies our viewer, I am very happy. I am not in favour of those who write off Yugoslavia so easily. I think that there is a lot of chance of putting things right, after clarifications have been made, and that a State could be set up of equal nations and nationalities as far as is possible, but I am not in favour of having somebody forced to stay in Yugoslavia -- everybody has the right to create a State as corresponds to his needs so nobody must be prevented from doing so, because any prevention will lead to problems, and conflict if you will. At all events, all nations in Yugoslavia should be allowed to create a State of their own as they see fit, as would correspond to their needs and in which they will be happy. We mentioned the National Council here -- we are not all members of the National Council in Sidski Banovci, which does not mean that we are not working for the interests of the Serbian people, and not only the Serb people -- we are in favour of having every nation who is jeopardised fought for -- that their rights become the rights -- equal to the rights of other nations. Question: Does the Serbian people have any reason to prevent Croats from having a State of their own?

utterances.speaker: MR. OCIC
utterances.text: No people can prevent or deny the legitimate right of every people to their own State. This goes for the Serbian people as well. No other people has the right to prevent the Serbs from creating their own State and of developing their economic resources. A large part of the Serbian people devoted their energies and were sacrificed to recreate other people's States. Whether we want to admit that or not the Serbian people created the first and second Yugoslavias. The Serbian people has morally more right -- maybe not politically more right -- to decide on the fate or break-up of Yugoslavia. If Yugoslavia was just a station they passed through en route to their own State which they were unable to create without the assistance of Serbs in 1918 and 1945, Serbs should not pay the price of creating other people's States, and the illusions today, we have paid the price."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honour, in the transcript, it is not clear that this gentleman is answering this question. It appears that Mr. Dokmanovic is the one providing the answer. The name has not been changed -- the name of this gentleman is Ocic -- I think it is clear to distinguish, because the purpose of this tape is to show what Mr. Dokmanovic had said, because he is the one being tried here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "So they have paid the price to keep the States of other peoples alive and the illusions have been paid dearly today, and we should not be slaves to those illusions. Everybody should be allowed to create the State that they want, and the Serbian people has that right. It cannot be denied to it. So I am in favour of a civilised parting of ways, and nobody can love each other by force. The only thing we should pay attention to is to minimise the costs, especially in terms of human life, and the threats coming from the other side, what Sime Djodan said, that one million Croats would die in order to exterminate the one million Serbs who live in Croatia, if that should come true. I think that no Serbs -- no Croats should die in order to create those States in the Serbian ethnic territory, and when they issue such genocidal threats to Serbian people, they forget that it is not only 1 million Serbs who live in Croatia, Serbs live elsewhere. If we were to take that to its logical limit, it would cause a spilling of blood -- that would not have any good consequences for anyone, so I am in favour of a Serbian State that would make it possible for everybody to live normally. People in Lika and Kordun, they have mental illness, because they have not the basic pre-conditions for their existence there. Question: Mr. Hadzic, do you believe that civilised parting ways that Mr. Ocic was telling us about was possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HADZIC
utterances.text: I am an optimist by nature and I thought it would be possible, as they said, to create a peaceful co-existence, but after the recent events I categorically state that any co-existence is impossible, it does not exist any more here and that the level of the presidency, they should have -- they should discuss some kind of peaceful parting of ways. I am not in favour of the break-up of Yugoslavia but, as Mr. Ocic said, can you imagine how the people in Croatia live after the events that we have seen on TV -- people just left their homes, and guarded their homes at night -- the police arrived -- those people did not have any weapons -- the police officer arrived, he is a Serb although he does not feel that he is a Serb, he made lists of all those people who stood there peacefully. It was all very cold, the night was very cold, but you can imagine how we lived there. So yesterday, at the meeting of the municipal committee, we decided to organise a meeting in the centre of Vukovar -- a meeting, a rally, which would be in support of the decisions of the presidency, and also to protest the failure to comply with those decisions of the presidency, because civilians are being armed and they are not returning their weapons. If they return their weapons, then they can get those weapons back in no time. Question: Now we will hear another viewer -- this is the third channel of the Novi Sad TV. You are on the air. Caller: I have been very upset with the TV programme I saw and some nights ago we saw the tapes that were filmed by the army about what was being prepared in Croatia and in Yugoslavia in general. From 1918 on Serbs have suffered the most, and then in 1948 there was this genocide against Serbs and gypsies and Jews. Has this been a lesson enough, that we should wait and have those things happen to us and that nobody reacts except for some individuals being called in for interrogation and the weapons, they are still in the houses of HDZ members and police stations -- only it is under some kind of supervision, so can we expect that we will have a peaceful night tonight and during the following nights, whether our wives and children are safe or maybe we should think that the civil war is about to break out any day now -- this army of ours, can it control such incidents and if they control those events, and if it issues an ultimatum for the weapons to be returned, and then the leadership who caused all this, can they be arrested and tried publicly instead of having all this hushed up? The Croatian Democratic Union never distanced itself. We are still in fear -- all of us who live here, and I am calling from Novi Sad, all of us who live in this area, we saw that map and we saw half of Vojvodina and Novi Sad was also included in the map, do we have to fear the civil war which is about to break out soon or does JNA have some kind of power in Yugoslavia where we want to live, or are we to be expecting the civil war to break out? Question: Mr. Petrovic, the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me just make an explanation -- whether the army has any power in the country. It is not very good to say that the army has some kind of power -- army has its task, its job, just like everybody else -- every other profession. If something were to happen as our viewer says, like the civil war, I would say that that would not be a civil war -- it would be a war of two polarised peoples -- Serbs -- Question: Well, let us not assume now, and create hypothetical situations? Answer: The Serbian people believe the JNA will protect it. The Serbian National Council gave its support in a proclamation a couple of days ago to the presidency and we hope that things will go back to normal. How the situation will evolve, of course -- it is a hypothetical situation. We are trying for the Serbian people to gather them together, we have called on them to exercise caution, and to keep their cool. It may seem easy to say so, but it is not easy. We all have our personal impulses, which may be in contradiction of that statement, but we believe that we will have a peaceful solution. I will now go back to 1943 and something that Mr. Franklin Roosevelt said at our Anglo-American convention having learned what was happening in the independent state of Croatia and the pogroms against the Serbian people at this time. He proposed the Croatian people should be placed under tutelage. A people that is unable to act rationally -- a people that acts irrationally -- that should be a minimum, for a people to be placed under tutelage. The American politicians said that at the time -- President Tudjman is probably aware of that and it is possible that he would just continue with his story that he is prepared to give up Spegelj and Bolkovac and all his leaders, so that in the end he can claim to be a Democrat, so that he retains his power, but I think that there should not be a war. Question: Mr. Matic, do you trust the Yugoslav People's Army, that it is capable of protecting Serbs in Slavonia, and Baranja and Knin and other parts of the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I profoundly believe that is possible from the aspects of the present day, but it is essential to know the situation on location. It is tense and dynamic there, and it has reached boiling point and I think that, unless these measures are consistently implemented, there will be an explosive incident, because there does not seem to be any authority which can retain and keep the people under control. Question: Mr. Ocic, I would like to hear you on that subject -- the Serbs have so many times been tricked throughout history that they have reason to doubt. How do you assess the confidence of the Serbian people in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. OCIC
utterances.text: Nothing else remains for the Serbs -- they must, and in view of their fighting traditions and everything else, they believe and wish to believe in the army and the army is their force, but it is not the army that is the problem. It is the presidency there to command the army and to bring decisions as to the final denouement, disentanglement of the situation, so it is the responsibility of the presidency and the presidency must act responsibly and quickly, otherwise the situation might escape our control and it will be difficult to bring life back to normal, so confidence in the army exists with the people, but the presidency must play its role. The vice-president of this presidency says one thing and another thing; this testifies to his role and responsibility -- he is playing his role very well and in fact he is realising his goal of great division of goals that other people are acting very successfully Spegelj and Boljkovac, Bobetko and Rukavina will probably come and I think that this type of Bolshevik thinking on the problem with regard to cadre cleansing does not solve the problem at all. The problem is more acute, and it is a question of the destiny and fate of the people. It is the problem of the State of the Yugoslavia, other new States. Therefore, with this sort of whitewashing operation or any other drive to mask the essence of the problem, it is no good. We must all confront the cruelty of reality and all the complexities of the real situation. We are -- and of the historical moment. Any cadre whitewashing or cleansing is a solution, only a superficial solution to the problem. In today's situation everybody has his role. All the Croatian politicians, whether they are in the presidency of Yugoslavia or in the Federal Executive Council or Government, or whether they have functions within Croatia -- this is a very good distribution of roles, they are highly, well synchronised and very effective and efficient. Question: Mr. Matic, I have one more question for you. Tudjman went to Austria recently, he asked that Austria recognise Croatia. The President of Austria, Waldheim, is not received by anyone in the world now -- does that testify to the international position in any way of the new Croatian State?

utterances.speaker: MR. MATIC
utterances.text: Well, probably Tudjman is trying to play a hand which was uncovered in Slovenia today to contact with the remains of the Habsburgs. Perhaps they wish to save their State and to create a State which will be recognised by a sort of abridged version of an Austro-Hungarian monarchy and that this is being masked under a combination of an Alpe-Adria organisation, but these are all suppositions and his travels through Europe and his writings are attempts to win over a vote for his independent State, because we must realise, understand, that, for deep historical complexes they do not know what they are about. It is a nation that has got a lot of complexes, and therefore belongs to the smallest of historical peoples. They live upon the concept of war, Catholicism against Orthodoxy -- this must not be forgotten. What is being done now by Otto Habsburg in the Parliament today might one day become the head of a revived Austro-Hungary, to call it that, and everything comes within the framework of an age-old plan to bring the inheritors of the monarchy, the Habsburg dynasty and the Carthesian war. Question: And in that context, Mr. Ocic, how do you view the smuggling of arms from Hungary?

utterances.speaker: MR. OCIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, everything that is unloyal should be brought before the law. If there are no elementary prerequisites for the economic life of people, if people have no ambition to undermine the country, then they will stop from living a normal life, whereas on the same count, smugglers are left to run amok, and this discrepancy and these smugglers, this smuggling testifies to the nature of Government and the conception of the rule of law in the State -- something that is proclaimed as a democracy but which is in fact a privatisation and pilfering towards the State itself. I do not know how you can have a State for example where there are only Croats, where this could be tolerated. It is something that is absolutely abnormal in any State. Question: And to draw our programme to a close for this evening, let us ask Mr. Koncarevic, the Secretary-General of the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, how he views the situation -- what solution he sees to Serbs living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, this evening, we have talked about the Serbian National Council. Today we have adopted the view and we shall be presenting the presidency with that view as to how to solve the problem. In Croatia, there is a disputed and undisputed territory -- undisputed territory is where the Croats had their ethnic majority before the beginning of the First World War. The disputed territory is that territory in the region of Krajina and Western Srem, Baranja, Slavonia and Moslavina. We proposed to the President of Yugoslavia that it suspend the competencies of the Croatian SABOR and leadership in all the territories where the Serbian people are living, because their elementary human rights are being jeopardised of the Serbian people and the basic right of man is the right to life and it is that right that is being jeopardised. Furthermore -- Speaker: Unfortunately, our time has run out, our programme is at the very end. These were members of the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. They are prominent Serbs from the region, and they presented their views on the topical situation in Croatia. Thank you for your attention, for viewing us, and good night."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise for you having to see things you did not have to see, but in the supporting material of the Prosecutor, the words said by Ilija Petrovic -- I do not know whether the President of America said those things or not -- that is not up to me to decide, but in the supporting material presented by the Prosecutor, these words were attributed to Slavko Dokmanovic and that is why it was important for you to see this as well as his statement as to whether he was or was not a member of the Serbian National Council. I tender this tape to be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I do not know what Mr. Fila is talking about and what we have attributed to Mr. Dokmanovic and what we have not. We have no objection to the tendering of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The tape is marked D67.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Niemann did not understand what I was saying. In a bag which I received at the very beginning of the trial as supporting material, there was an article from the Croatian press where those things were stated -- the ones that I just explained here. The reports were incorrect. I will have no more tapes for you. The only thing that remains is this last issue -- the BBC tape -- it is three hours long. I still think that we should see it, but only if the Prosecutor agrees -- I would then be tendering that as evidence, as some kind of a joint defence -- joint exhibit, if the Prosecutor objects, then I will not be seeking to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if Mr. Fila wishes to tender the tape, he may do so, but we are not doing it by way of a joint exercise. We do not have any particular objection to the BBC programme, except that it is a programme which has been made and edited by producers in the BBC to present a particular point of view. I am not suggesting it is wrong or there is anything incorrect in that, but I cannot see how the court can be much assisted by it. It is entertaining and extremely interesting and basically is rather much in line with the Prosecution view anyway, but I think your Honours are better assisted by hearing evidence from witnesses who can testify to these events, rather than see something that has been produced by the BBC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We agree with the Prosecutor. I think probably there is no point in viewing this BBC programme. We do not want to be influenced, it has been edited by people. And also because we need time to hear the evidence to be produced by the Defence counsel -- the witnesses you are going to call in May. We may run out of time. Therefore, for the sake also of saving time, let us do without this tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw my proposal. When the Prosecutor tendered those two photographs I said immediately that it may or may not be interesting to you -- since you do not deem it to be interesting, I withdraw my proposal and that would conclude the proposals of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is one matter that I thought I might raise at this stage, if I could. It relates to our next session in either the next session or the session in May. What we would like to do is, rather than simply wait until the June sittings to present the case in rebuttal, if Mr. Fila reaches the end of his case earlier than he expects -- it may or may not happen -- there is some rebuttal evidence that we could present in that time, so I would just like at this early stage to indicate that, should Mr. Fila run short of witnesses, that we would be happy to step in at that stage and could step in at that stage and fill the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said right at the very beginning that I, as the lead counsel, allow that whatever the Prosecutor deems to be necessary to tender into evidence, they can do so and I will not raise any objections, if it is true that we are here to determine the truth, and I think it is. So I raise no objections now and I will raise no objections in the future. The only thing is that I would like to be told in advance what the evidence is. As I said yesterday, I have the right to a rejoinder, since from the times of the ancient Rome, the Defence has the right to speak the last -- to be heard the last, but not twice, as it was in your Senate, your Honour -- of course in the times of Julius Caesar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The point however raised by Mr. Niemann was whether you would accept that the rebuttal evidence be heard in May without waiting until June and I see that you do agree -- if you complete your case, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Fila has a good point, namely, that he would like to take a look at the witness statements and I think of the rebuttal witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means we will notify Mr. Fila of the evidence we anticipate to call. I should make sure I stated the matter precisely, though, from our point of view. We would not be expected to present all of it, it is just we have some available now that we can present. Until we have heard the full Defence case we are not in a position to say the totality of it. Just because Judge May raised it on the last occasion, we are not expecting anything terribly extensive in rebuttal evidence. If it happens we have some time in May, that will significantly reduce any amount of time we need in June -- that is the only point we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sorry, my only concern is that this should prejudice the Defence -- that the Prosecution would present its rebuttal case and, as you know, I live in Belgrade and I have my evidence stored there and not here. I need some time to learn what the Prosecution is about to present so I can make my own decisions so I am not caught by surprised, to put it very simply, and that is all. I think it is only fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I hope that we all agree that our main goal should be to finish this trial by 18 June, at the latest -- I think this is important. If you need time for your rejoinder, of course we will go on to July -- we will continue in July. We would then have only one week probably available in July, but if it is possible without in any case restricting the rights of Defence to finish in June, I think this would be in the best interests of the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will be concluding my case in June -- I just wanted to see what the Prosecution will present in May so that I can say what I want to say in June. I do not need July at all. Thank you very much, but I do not need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is agreed. I hope that we will also take up a suggestion made by Mr. Fila about the closing statements -- I wonder whether the Prosecutor is prepared also, in the way of the positive suggestion by Mr. Fila -- Mr. Fila suggested, if possible, closing statements should be handed in, in writing, and then of course you will make an oral statement which could be much shorter than the written one. Let us see whether it is possible for the Prosecutor as well to do so, with a view to shortening the length of the trial. We adjourn now and resume our hearings on 18 May. (At 12.10 p.m. the matter adjourned until 18 May 1998) 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
